title: Schedules, Serializability & Recoverability
summary: When multiple transactions run at the same time, the order of their reads and writes matters. Learn how to tell a safe schedule from a dangerous one.

blocks.markdown:
A **schedule** is the actual order in which database operations from multiple transactions execute — reads, writes, commits, aborts, all interleaved.

- The goal: concurrent execution should look as if transactions ran one at a time.
- Two tests matter: **serializability** (correct outcome) and **recoverability** (safe rollback).
- These properties underpin every locking and timestamp protocol. See [concurrency-control](concurrency-control) and [transactions-acid](transactions-acid).

blocks.subTitle: Serial vs concurrent
blocks.markdown:
A **serial schedule** runs all operations of T1, then all of T2 — no interleaving. Always correct, but blocks concurrency and wastes CPU while a transaction waits on I/O.

A **concurrent schedule** interleaves operations from multiple transactions. It can be faster, but may produce wrong results if not controlled.

The challenge: allow interleaving while guaranteeing the same outcome as some serial order.

blocks.subTitle: Why interleaving needs control
blocks.markdown:
Without control, concurrent schedules break correctness:

- **Dirty read** — T2 reads a value T1 wrote but hasn't committed; T1 aborts → T2 used invalid data.
- **Lost update** — T1 and T2 both read X=100, both add 50, both write 150. One update is lost.
- **Unrepeatable read** — T1 reads X, T2 updates X, T1 reads X again and gets a different value.

These are the classic [transactions-acid](transactions-acid) isolation failures.

Two operations **conflict** if they are from **different transactions**, target the **same data item**, and **at least one is a write**. The three conflict pairs:

- Read-Write (one reads, other writes)
- Write-Read (one writes, other reads)
- Write-Write (both write)

A schedule is **conflict serializable** if it can be transformed into a serial schedule by swapping non-conflicting operations. This is the standard correctness test.

blocks.subTitle: Example
blocks.markdown:
Schedule: `R1(A) W2(A) W1(A) W2(B)` — T1 reads A, T2 writes A, T1 writes A, T2 writes B.

- R1(A) vs W2(A): conflict (different transactions, same item, one write) → T1 must precede T2 on A.
- W1(A) vs W2(A): conflict → T1 must precede T2 on A. Consistent.
- W2(B) has no conflict with T1.

No contradiction → this schedule is conflict serializable (equivalent to T1→T2).

The **precedence graph** (serialization graph) tests conflict serializability mechanically.

**Build it:** one node per transaction. Draw edge Ti → Tj if any operation of Ti conflicts with a later operation of Tj.

**Rule:** the schedule is conflict serializable **if and only if the graph has no cycle**.

blocks.subTitle: Reading the result
blocks.markdown:
If the graph is **acyclic**, do a topological sort of the nodes — that gives you the equivalent serial order.

- Acyclic graph with T1→T2→T3: equivalent serial schedule is T1, T2, T3.
- A cycle means the schedule demands contradictory orderings (T1 before T2 **and** T2 before T1) — impossible to serialize.

This is O(V+E) and is how most real concurrency-control analyses work.

**View serializability** is a broader correctness notion. Schedule S is view serializable if it is **view equivalent** to some serial schedule — meaning:

1. Each transaction reads the same initial value (or the same writer's value) as in the serial schedule.
2. The final write on each data item is done by the same transaction.

Every conflict-serializable schedule is also view serializable, but **not vice versa**. Testing view serializability is NP-complete, so conflict serializability (precedence graph) is what DBMSs use in practice.

blocks.subTitle: Recoverable schedules
blocks.markdown:
Serializability is about **correctness of reads and writes**. Recoverability is about **safe undo**.

A schedule is **recoverable** if: whenever T2 reads a value written by T1, T1 must **commit before T2 commits**.

If T1 aborts after T2 has already committed, T2's committed state is based on data that never existed — an unrecoverable situation. Recoverable schedules prevent this.

blocks.subTitle: Cascading rollback
blocks.markdown:
**Cascading rollback** happens when T1 aborts and forces all transactions that read T1's uncommitted values to also abort — which may force more aborts in a chain.

Example: T1 writes X → T2 reads X → T3 reads X. T1 aborts → T2 must abort → T3 must abort. One abort rolls back three transactions, wasting all their work.

This is recoverable but costly. DBMSs try to avoid it entirely with stricter schedules.

blocks.subTitle: Cascadeless & strict
blocks.markdown:
Three levels, each stricter:

| Schedule type | Rule | Allows cascading rollback? |
|---|---|---|
| Recoverable | Commit order: writer before reader | Yes |
| Cascadeless | Read only committed values | No |
| Strict | Read/write only after writer commits | No, and simplest undo |

**Strict** is what most real systems target — undo is a simple overwrite of the before-image without tracing dependencies.

blocks.subTitle: Why cascadeless matters
blocks.markdown:
A **cascadeless schedule** says: a transaction may only read a data item after the transaction that last wrote it has **committed**.

- This eliminates dirty reads entirely.
- No dirty reads → no cascading abort chain.
- Strict schedules add the same rule for **writes** too: don't write an item another transaction has written until that transaction commits.

SS2PL (strict two-phase locking) enforces strict schedules automatically. See [concurrency-control](concurrency-control).

blocks.subTitle: What is a schedule
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a schedule in database concurrency?**

A **schedule** is the ordered sequence of operations (reads, writes, commits, aborts) from multiple concurrent transactions as they actually execute on the database. It captures the real interleaving, not just the per-transaction logic.

blocks.subTitle: Conflict serializability test
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you test whether a schedule is conflict serializable?**

Build a **precedence (serialization) graph**: one node per transaction, draw Ti→Tj for every conflicting pair where Ti's operation comes first. If the graph is **acyclic**, the schedule is conflict serializable and the topological sort gives the equivalent serial order. A cycle means it is not.

blocks.subTitle: Recoverable vs cascadeless vs strict
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between recoverable, cascadeless, and strict schedules?**

**Recoverable**: if T2 read from T1, T1 must commit before T2 — prevents permanent dirty state.
**Cascadeless**: transactions only read **committed** values — eliminates dirty reads and cascading aborts.
**Strict**: also delays writes on items held by uncommitted transactions — makes undo trivially a before-image overwrite.

Strict ⊂ Cascadeless ⊂ Recoverable. Real systems target strict.
